subject: Autoregressive model: problem with the first year

messages.author: 54e08ddecb38c1b3
messages.subject: Autoregressive model: problem with the first year
parts:
I am trying to translate a density-dependent population model from JAGS to Stan, but am having some trouble. I have dumbed down my model to make the transition easier but I am still having issues. 

The model and parameters are outlined below. The true (or latent) duck population in each area is correlated to the population in that area the year before and some climatic covariables. 

[Y] is duck populations inventoried each year
[Z] are the regions in which populations are inventoried
Obs_ducks is the annual population estimate
sigma_ducks is the standard error of that estimate
true_ducks is the latent population in each year. 
  
My problem is related to the lag effect induced by the density dependence.  Right now I can run the model below only if I "fix" the latent numbers of ducks to the numbers of ducks that were estimated during the first year. 

If I try to replace the line 
true_ducks[1,z] <- Obs_ducks[1,z];   //First year

with the line 
true_ducks[1,z] ~ normal(Obs_ducks[1,z], sigma_ducks[1,z]);   //First year

My R session crashes. I have also tried running the model without any input about the first year like it is suggested in the manual but my R session crashed with this solution as well.

To get the model running I supply own initial values.  The initial values for rg, dd, sigma2, beta and sigma ducks are randomly drawn from uniform distributions and I use the estimated population as initial values for true_ducks. 

Any suggestions to make the first year of the model stochastic would be greatly appreciated.

Chris 

####The model
data{
  int<lower=0> Z;  // n Areas
  int<lower=0> Y;  // n Years
  real Obs_ducks[Y,Z]; //n observed birds
  real<lower=0> sigma_ducks[Y,Z]; //s.e. on observations
  real Summer[Y,Z]; //climate covar
  real Autumn[Y,Z]; //climate covar
  real Winter[Y,Z]; //climate covar
  real Spring[Y,Z]; //climate covar
}
parameters {
  real rg[Z]; //specific growth rate
  real<lower=-20, upper=2> dd[Z]; // strength density dependence
  real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma2[Z]; //process variance 
  real beta[Z,4]; //climate effect
  real shock_ducks[(Y-1),Z]; //demographic stochasticity
}
transformed parameters {
  real Sg[Z];   //Stochastic Growth rate
  real sigma[Z];  //sd variance
  for (z in 1:Z){
    Sg[z] <- rg[z] - 0.5*sigma2[z];
    sigma[z] <- sqrt(sigma2[z]);
  }
}
model{
  matrix[Y,Z] true_ducks; //true birds population
  matrix[(Y-1),Z] delta_log_ducks;   //pop growth on the log scale
  matrix[(Y-1),Z] Zeta;    //total climate effects
  rg ~ normal(0, 1000); 
  dd ~ uniform(-20, 2); 
  sigma2 ~ uniform(0,100);
  for (z in 1:Z){
    beta[z,1]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,2]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,3]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,4]~ normal(0, 1000);
    true_ducks[1,z] <- Obs_ducks[1,z];   //First year
    for (t in 2:Y){
      Zeta[t-1,z] <- beta[z,1]*Summer[t,z] + beta[z,2]*Autumn[t,z] + beta[z,3]*Winter[t,z] + beta[z,4]*Spring[t,z];
      delta_log_ducks[t-1,z] <- Sg[z] - dd[z]*log(true_ducks[t-1,z]);
      shock_ducks[t-1,z] ~ normal(0, sigma[z]);
      true_ducks[t,z] <- exp(log(true_ducks[t-1,z]) + delta_log_ducks[t-1,z]+ Zeta[t-1,z] + shock_ducks[t-1,z]);  
      Obs_ducks[t,z] ~ normal(true_ducks[t,z], sigma_ducks[t,z]); 
    }
  }
}

parts:
Maybe a made an error in translating my code from JAGS to STAN?

The population of ducks at time 1 is a parameter for population at time 2.
delta_log_ducks[t-1,z] <- Sg[z] - dd[z]*log(true_ducks[t-1,z]);
true_ducks[t,z] <- exp(log(true_ducks[t-1,z]) + delta_log_ducks[t-1,z]+ Zeta[t-1,z] + shock_ducks[t-1,z]);

I could in theory I guess I could fit the exact same model at year 1 that I fit for all  the other years but then my population at year 1 would be dependent on year 0 for which I have no information. Instead I would rather use the information I have at year 1 (i.e the population estimates and s.e.) to start the model.

In his current form the model has to start at a definitive value (i.e the population estimate at year 1) which bugs me a bit. I would rather acknowledge the uncertainty in the populations estimate and draw the population at year 1 from a normal distribution with the s.e that has been estimated from the survey. 

My apologies if I sound a little dense. 

Chris

Wow! that is embarrassing... 

With that in mind I rewrote part of my model. I will post it below for posterity in case another newbie make such a silly mistake. It's still a bit clunky but I feel like I'm on the right path.

Thank you for your time Jiqiang. 

Chris
#####

data{
  int<lower=0> Z;  // n Areas

int<lower=0> T;  // n Years
  real Obs_ducks[T,Z]; //n observed birds population
  real<lower=0> sigma_ducks[T,Z]; //s.e. on observations
  real Summer[T,Z]; //climate covar
  real Autumn[T,Z]; //climate covar
  real Winter[T,Z]; //climate covar
  real Spring[T,Z]; //climate covar

}
parameters {
  real rg[Z]; //specific growth rate
  real<lower=-20, upper=2> dd[Z]; //strength densitydependence
real<lower=0, upper=10> sigma2[Z]; //process variance
real beta[Z,4]; //climate effect

real shock_ducks[(T-1),Z]; //demographic stochasticity
  real year1 [Z];

}
transformed parameters {
  real Sg[Z];   //Stochastic Growth rate
  real sigma[Z];  //sd variance

matrix [T,Z] true_ducks; //true birds population
  matrix[(T-1),Z] delta_log_ducks;   //pop growth on the log scale
  matrix[(T-1),Z] Zeta;    //total climate effects

for (z in 1:Z){
      Sg[z] <- rg[z] - 0.5*sigma2[z];
      sigma[z] <- sqrt(sigma2[z]);

true_ducks[1,z] <- year1[z];
      for (t in 2:T){
Zeta[t-1,z] <- beta[z,1]*Summer[t,z] + beta[z,2]*Autumn[t,z] + beta[z,3]*Winter[t,z] + beta[z,4]*Spring[t,z];

delta_log_ducks[t-1,z] <- Sg[z] - dd[z]*log(true_ducks[t-1,z]);
        true_ducks[t,z] <- exp(log(true_ducks[t-1,z]) + delta_log_ducks[t-1,z]+ Zeta[t-1,z] + shock_ducks[t-1,z]);  
      }
  }
}
model{
for (z in 1:Z){

rg ~ uniform(-20, 2); 
    dd[z] ~ normal(0, 1); 
    sigma2[z] ~ inv_gamma(1,1);

beta[z,1]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,2]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,3]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,4]~ normal(0, 1000);

year1[z] ~ normal(Obs_ducks[1,z], sigma_ducks[1,z]); 
    for (t in 2:T){
shock_ducks[t-1,z] ~ normal(0, sigma[z]);

Obs_ducks[t,z] ~ normal(true_ducks[t,z], sigma_ducks[t,z]); 
    }
  }
}

parts: I have statisticsl (not computational) problems with the following lines of code:

sigma2[z] ~ inv_gamma(1,1);
    beta[z,1]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,2]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,3]~ normal(0, 1000);
    beta[z,4]~ normal(0, 1000);

I don't like the inv_gamma prior for reasons discussed in my 2006 paper in Bayesian Analysis.
I don't like the N(0,1000) priors because they are too weak.  I'd prefer something like N(0,10) (although I haven't looked at the model or data carefully to see if "10" is in fact ok, my more general point is that it's a good idea to regularize coefs a bit).

A

There are some issues with the posted model after a glance. 

First, there is no restraint on parameters on which a uniform prior is specified.  Please see
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/VonPUkdcZuUJ

Second, some statements can be vectorized to improve speed, see the stan manual or https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ.  A simple example is that you can just replace the following
for (z in 1:Z){
dd[z] ~ normal(0, 1);

}

with `dd ~ normal(0, 1); '

--
Jiqiang

> I have statisticsl (not computational) problems with the following lines of code:
>
> sigma2[z] ~ inv_gamma(1,1);
> beta[z,1]~ normal(0, 1000);
> beta[z,2]~ normal(0, 1000);
> beta[z,3]~ normal(0, 1000);
> beta[z,4]~ normal(0, 1000);
>
> I don't like the inv_gamma prior for reasons discussed in my 2006 paper in Bayesian Analysis.
> I don't like the N(0,1000) priors because they are too weak. I'd prefer something like N(0,10) (although I haven't
> looked at the model or data carefully to see if "10" is in fact ok, my more general point is that it's a good idea to
> regularize coefs a bit).

As I mentioned in an earlier post, this will also help
immensely with stability of the sampler as it won't be
allowed to drift around in places where you don't want
it to be (like a regression coefficient of 500!).

- Bob

On Thu, Dec 13, 2012 at 1:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On 12/12/12 4:12 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I have statisticsl (not computational) problems with the following lines of code:

     sigma2[z] ~ inv_gamma(1,1);
     beta[z,1]~ normal(0, 1000);
     beta[z,2]~ normal(0, 1000);
     beta[z,3]~ normal(0, 1000);
     beta[z,4]~ normal(0, 1000);

I don't like the inv_gamma prior for reasons discussed in my 2006 paper in Bayesian Analysis.
I don't like the N(0,1000) priors because they are too weak.  I'd prefer something like N(0,10) (although I haven't
looked at the model or data carefully to see if "10" is in fact ok, my more general point is that it's a good idea to
regularize coefs a bit).

As I mentioned in an earlier post, this will also help
immensely with stability of the sampler as it won't be
allowed to drift around in places where you don't want
it to be (like a regression coefficient of 500!).

- Bob
